question: What are SQL Joins and how do they work?
answer: SQL Joins combine rows from two or more tables based on a related column. INNER JOIN returns only matching rows from both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table plus matching rows from the right (nulls where no match). RIGHT JOIN is the opposite. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both tables. CROSS JOIN returns every combination (cartesian product). Joins are the foundation of relational databases — without them you cannot fetch related data.
example: Think of two registers at a school — one for students and one for exam marks. INNER JOIN is like matching students who have marks — if a student has no marks, they are excluded. LEFT JOIN shows ALL students, even those who missed the exam (their marks column shows NULL). RIGHT JOIN shows ALL marks entries, even if the student was deleted from the students register.
codeSnippet:
-- Sample Tables
-- Students: Id, Name, ClassId
-- Classes: Id, ClassName
-- Marks: Id, StudentId, Subject, Score

-- INNER JOIN: Only students who have a class assigned
SELECT s.Name, c.ClassName
FROM Students s
INNER JOIN Classes c ON s.ClassId = c.Id;

-- LEFT JOIN: All students, even those without a class
SELECT s.Name, c.ClassName
FROM Students s
LEFT JOIN Classes c ON s.ClassId = c.Id;
-- Students without a class will show NULL for ClassName

-- Multiple Joins: Students + Class + Marks
SELECT s.Name, c.ClassName, m.Subject, m.Score
FROM Students s
INNER JOIN Classes c ON s.ClassId = c.Id
LEFT JOIN Marks m ON m.StudentId = s.Id;

-- Self Join: Employee and their Manager (same table)
SELECT e.Name AS Employee, m.Name AS Manager
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN Employees m ON e.ManagerId = m.Id;

-- Join with Aggregation
SELECT c.ClassName, COUNT(s.Id) AS StudentCount, AVG(m.Score) AS AvgScore
FROM Classes c
LEFT JOIN Students s ON s.ClassId = c.Id
LEFT JOIN Marks m ON m.StudentId = s.Id
GROUP BY c.ClassName
ORDER BY AvgScore DESC;

-- In EF Core (LINQ equivalent)
var result = await _db.Students
    .Include(s => s.Class)         // INNER JOIN Classes
    .Include(s => s.Marks)         // LEFT JOIN Marks
    .Where(s => s.Class.ClassName == "10th")
    .Select(s => new {
        s.Name,
        Class = s.Class.ClassName,
        TotalMarks = s.Marks.Sum(m => m.Score)
    })
    .ToListAsync();
steps: INNER JOIN — returns only rows that match in BOTH tables
LEFT JOIN — returns ALL rows from left table + matching from right
RIGHT JOIN — returns ALL rows from right table + matching from left
FULL OUTER JOIN — returns ALL rows from both tables
CROSS JOIN — returns every combination (rarely used)
Self Join — table joined with itself (e.g., employee-manager)
Always use ON clause to specify the join condition
In EF Core, use .Include() for joins and .ThenInclude() for nested
Use LEFT JOIN when you want all records even without matches

question: What is API Versioning in .NET Web API?
answer: API Versioning lets you maintain multiple versions of your API at the same time. When you need to change an API response or behavior, you create a new version instead of breaking existing clients. Old clients continue using v1, new clients use v2. You can version via URL path (/api/v1/products), query string (?api-version=1.0), or HTTP headers. The Asp.Versioning.Mvc package makes this easy in .NET.
example: API Versioning is like a restaurant updating its menu. They don't throw away the old menu overnight — regular customers still want their favourite dishes. Instead, they introduce a 'New Menu' (v2) while keeping the 'Classic Menu' (v1) available. Over time, they can retire the old menu when all customers have switched.

Configure AddApiVersioning() in Program.cs with default version

Header: X-Api-Version: 2.0 — keeps URL clean
Use [ApiVersion('1.0')] attribute on controllers
Create separate controllers for each version

question: What is Background Job Processing in .NET using Hangfire?
answer: Background jobs are tasks that run outside the normal HTTP request-response cycle. If a user places an order, you don't want to make them wait while you send confirmation emails, generate invoices, or update inventory. You process these tasks in the background. Hangfire is a popular .NET library for background job processing. It supports fire-and-forget jobs, delayed jobs, recurring jobs, and continuations. It stores job info in a database and has a built-in dashboard.
example: Background jobs are like giving your clothes to a laundry service. You drop off the clothes (create a job) and go home (API returns response). The laundry (Hangfire) washes, irons, and delivers later in the background. You don't stand there waiting for each shirt to be washed. Recurring jobs are like a daily newspaper subscription — it happens automatically every day without you asking.
steps: Background jobs run tasks outside the HTTP request cycle
Install Hangfire and a storage provider (SqlServer, PostgreSql, etc.)
Register: AddHangfire() + AddHangfireServer() in Program.cs
Fire-and-Forget: BackgroundJob.Enqueue() — runs once immediately
Delayed: BackgroundJob.Schedule() — runs after specified time
Recurring: RecurringJob.AddOrUpdate() — runs on CRON schedule
Continuation: BackgroundJob.ContinueJobWith() — runs after another job
Dashboard at /hangfire shows all jobs, statuses, and history
Jobs are retried automatically on failure — configurable retries

question: What are SQL Indexes and how do they improve query performance?
answer: An index in SQL is like an index in a textbook — it helps the database find rows quickly without scanning the entire table. Without an index, the database performs a full table scan (reads every row) to find your data. With an index, it jumps directly to the matching rows. Indexes are critical for WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY columns. However, indexes slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE because the index also needs to be updated. So you should only index columns that are frequently searched or filtered.
example: Imagine a phone directory with 10 lakh entries. Without an index (alphabetical order), to find 'Sharma' you would have to read every single entry from the beginning — that could take hours. With an alphabetical index, you jump directly to 'S' section and find 'Sharma' in seconds. But if you insert a new name, the directory needs to be re-sorted — that is the cost of maintaining indexes.
steps: Index = data structure that speeds up row lookup in a table
Without index: Full Table Scan — reads every row (slow)
With index: Index Seek — jumps to matching rows (fast)
Create index on columns used in WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY
Composite index covers multiple columns — order matters
Unique index also prevents duplicate values
INCLUDE columns make a covering index — avoids table lookup
Too many indexes slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations
In EF Core: use .HasIndex() in OnModelCreating()

question: What is Rate Limiting in .NET Web API?
answer: Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make to your API within a time window. It protects your API from abuse, DDoS attacks, and overloading. For example, you can allow 100 requests per minute per user. If they exceed the limit, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests. .NET 7+ has built-in rate limiting middleware with four algorithms: Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket, and Concurrency limiter.
example: Rate limiting is like a ticket counter at a railway station. The counter (API) can serve only 10 customers (requests) per minute. If 20 people come at once, the first 10 get served and the rest are told 'Please wait and try again later' (429 status). This prevents the counter from being overwhelmed and ensures fair service for everyone.
steps: Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make per time window
Returns 429 Too Many Requests when limit exceeded
Fixed Window: simple counter that resets after each window
Sliding Window: smoother, avoids burst at window boundaries
Token Bucket: allows short bursts, refills tokens over time
Configure: builder.Services.AddRateLimiter() in Program.cs
Apply globally with app.UseRateLimiter() middleware
Apply per-endpoint: [EnableRateLimiting('policy')] attribute
Protects against DDoS, brute force attacks, and API abuse

question: What is Dependency Injection in .NET and what are service lifetimes?
answer: Dependency Injection (DI) in .NET means instead of creating objects manually with 'new', the framework creates and provides them for you. You register services in Program.cs and .NET injects them via constructor parameters. There are three service lifetimes: Transient (new instance every time), Scoped (one instance per HTTP request), and Singleton (one instance for the entire app lifetime). Choosing the right lifetime is critical — using the wrong one can cause bugs, memory leaks, or stale data.
example: Think of a restaurant. Singleton is the restaurant building — there is only one, shared by everyone, and it exists the entire time. Scoped is like a table setup — each customer group (HTTP request) gets their own table setup, and it is cleaned after they leave. Transient is like tissue paper — every time someone asks, they get a fresh piece. You would not reuse tissue paper, and you would not rebuild the restaurant for each customer.
steps: DI means the framework creates and provides dependencies for you
Register services in Program.cs: AddTransient, AddScoped, AddSingleton
Transient: new instance every injection — lightweight, stateless services
Scoped: one instance per HTTP request — DbContext, request-level services
Singleton: one instance for entire app — caching, configuration, logging
Inject via constructor: public MyController(IService service)
Always use interfaces (IService) not concrete classes — easier to test
NEVER inject Scoped service into Singleton — causes captive dependency bug
DbContext is Scoped by default — do not register it as Singleton
